hazards.blocked-exit: The hand truck is parked square across the cellar door. This room has one way out and a gas hazard that pools at floor level with no smell to warn you; nothing gets left leaning on, loaded against or blocking that door while anyone is working inside it.
hazards.hot-coupler-pull: You popped the quick-release straight off the manifold instead of bleeding the line down first. A coupler released under full line pressure throws beer and gas hard enough to catch you in the face at exactly the height you're crouched to; the pressure comes off slowly, at the regulator, before anything unlocks.
hazards.solo-lift: You reached to lift the second full keg without the hand truck. A full keg runs over 160 lb in an awkward round shape with nothing to grip, and UNITE HERE Local 2's own safety language calls for the hand truck or a two-person lift for precisely that reason — not because it can't be done once, but because a back injury from one bad lift ends a season, not a shift.
hazards.unchained-cylinder: That spare CO2 cylinder is standing free against the wall, not chained to a bracket. A cellar is a small, low-ceilinged room, and a cylinder that topples can shear its own valve on the way down — a snapped valve on a full bottle empties an asphyxiant gas into the room in seconds, which is exactly the failure NIOSH's cellar guidance is written against.

interrupts.alert: The manager leans down the cellar stairs: "Bar's slammed — how much longer on that keg?" — while you're still in the brace.
interrupts.cue: Wave him off on the house phone. The lift finishes the way it started.
interrupts.missNote: You stood the keg up early to answer him and finished the lift out of a bad crouch. The bar being busy upstairs was never actually the barback's decision to make about how this lift gets done.
interrupts.why: A rushed lift out of a half-finished brace is exactly how a strained back happens, and it costs the bar a lot more than the extra thirty seconds does — the right answer to being hurried mid-lift is telling the person hurrying you to wait, not skipping the part of the lift that protects you.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the house phone by the stairs. Call up that you'll be a minute — don't cut the brace short to answer him in person.

interrupts.alert: The cellar CO2 monitor behind you has gone into alarm. The reading is climbing, not settling.
interrupts.cue: Leave now. The monitor isn't a switch you reset from in here.
interrupts.missNote: You kept working the line while the monitor alarmed behind you. Carbon dioxide at a dangerous concentration gives you no smell and very little warning before it affects judgement — the people it hurts are the ones who decided to finish the step first.
interrupts.why: CO2 pools first at floor level, exactly where the manifold and your own crouch both are, so an alarm mid-change means the air you're breathing right now is already suspect — NIOSH's guidance treats every cellar alarm as real and leaving as the only correct first response, worked out from outside the room, not argued with from inside it.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the door, not the monitor. Resetting or silencing the sensor from the same spot that raised the alarm does nothing about the gas that's still in the room — the answer is leaving.

lateNotes.cellar-door: The door gets propped on the way out, once the change is finished and logged.
lateNotes.full-coupler: The coupler goes on the full keg only after it is seated in the socket — there is nothing to lock onto before that.
lateNotes.leak-gauge: The leak check comes after the coupler is on and snug, not before — there is no joint made yet to test.
lateNotes.purge-valve: The line gets purged after the leak check reads clean, not before — purging past a leak just blows the leak through faster.

name: Keg Cellar CO2

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the wall monitor and commit while it reads inside the clean-air band.

gauge.label: CELLAR CO₂
gauge.missNote: Above the clean-air band — do not start the change. Ventilate the cellar and read it again before touching a cylinder.

steps.prompt: Check the wall monitor and commit while it reads inside the clean-air band.
steps.title: Read the cellar CO2 monitor before going in
steps.why: CO2 is heavier than air and has no smell at a dangerous concentration, so the monitor is the only thing in this room that actually knows what you'd be breathing at floor level. NIOSH and Cal/OSHA both treat that reading, taken before the door is even opened for work, as the first control in the whole procedure — not a formality after it.

steps.cue: Check the restraint chain on the CO2 bottle and the nitrogen bottle before you touch either regulator.
steps.prompt: Check the restraint chain on the CO2 bottle and the nitrogen bottle before you touch either regulator.
steps.title: Confirm both gas cylinders are chained upright
steps.why: A compressed-gas cylinder that isn't chained is one bump from becoming a projectile with the neck sheared off, and the Compressed Gas Association's own handling practice — which Cal/OSHA's hazard communication rule backs with the cylinder's own safety data sheet — starts every job with a look at whether the chain is actually doing its job, not just present.

steps.cue: Read the high-pressure gauge on the CO2 regulator and commit inside the working band.

gauge.label: TANK PSI
gauge.missNote: Outside the working band — re-read the gauge before you commit to the change.

steps.prompt: Read the high-pressure gauge on the CO2 regulator and commit inside the working band.
steps.title: Check the regulator's tank pressure
steps.why: The tank-side gauge tells you how much gas is actually left behind the regulator before you commit to a whole keg change on it; running a cellar dry mid-service is a bar with no working taps, and the five seconds it takes to read this gauge is what keeps that from being a surprise.

steps.cue: Turn the coupler a quarter turn to unlock it from the spent keg.
steps.prompt: Turn the coupler a quarter turn to unlock it from the spent keg.
steps.title: Release the coupler from the empty keg
steps.why: The coupler is the only thing standing between the gas line and the keg's own residual pressure, so it comes off with a controlled quarter turn against the lock, never levered or forced — a coupler cracked loose under pressure is the same face-height spray as pulling it off a live line.

steps.cue: Hold a proper crouch — knees bent, keg close to the body — before anything comes off the floor.
steps.holdBreakNote: You stood up out of the brace before the count finished. Set it again — the lift starts from the crouch, not partway out of it.
steps.prompt: Hold a proper crouch — knees bent, keg close to the body — before anything comes off the floor.
steps.title: Brace before the lift
steps.why: A full keg is over 160 lb held at arm's length if you let it get away from your body, and the brace is what keeps the lift in your legs instead of your lower back; this is the same five seconds UNITE HERE Local 2's safety training spends on every keg station, because it is the one habit that keeps barbacks working past forty.

steps.cue: Carry the spent keg clear of the manifold and set it on the empty rack.

drag.missNote: Not on the rack — set the empty down square on the rack, not leaning against it.

steps.prompt: Carry the spent keg clear of the manifold and set it on the empty rack.
steps.title: Roll the empty keg to the empty rack
steps.why: The spent keg comes off the socket before the full one goes anywhere near it — working two kegs' worth of weight through the same footprint at once is exactly how a barback ends up pinned against the rack by one of them.

steps.cue: Roll the full keg from the storage rack, upright, and seat it on the manifold socket.

drag.missNote: Not seated on the socket — bring the keg square under the coupler before it goes anywhere near the line.

steps.prompt: Roll the full keg from the storage rack, upright, and seat it on the manifold socket.
steps.title: Bring the full keg onto the manifold socket
steps.why: This is the lift the brace was for: upright, close to the body, using the hand truck's own wheels for the distance rather than walking it on its rim, and set down square so the coupler lines up on the first try instead of the third.

steps.cue: Seat the coupler on the new keg's valve and turn it a quarter turn to lock.
steps.prompt: Seat the coupler on the new keg's valve and turn it a quarter turn to lock.
steps.title: Lock the coupler onto the full keg
steps.why: A coupler that stops short of the lock detent looks connected and isn't — it holds until the first surge of pressure, and then it lets go under whoever is standing over it, which by then is usually the next barback, not you.

steps.cue: Watch the line-pressure gauge hold steady and commit while it reads inside the sealed band.

gauge.label: LINE PSI
gauge.missNote: Pressure's not holding — that coupler isn't fully seated. Re-seat it and check again before purging anything.

steps.prompt: Watch the line-pressure gauge hold steady and commit while it reads inside the sealed band.
steps.title: Check the line gauge for a leak
steps.why: A coupler that isn't fully seated bleeds pressure slowly enough that the keg still pours, right up until the night it doesn't — reading the line gauge here, before the line ever gets purged or poured from, is how a slow leak gets caught as a five-second check instead of a flooded cellar floor.

steps.cue: Hold the purge valve open until the line runs clean gas, not the flat beer left in it from the last keg.
steps.holdBreakNote: You let go before the line ran clean. A partial purge still has the old beer in it — hold it the full count.
steps.prompt: Hold the purge valve open until the line runs clean gas, not the flat beer left in it from the last keg.
steps.title: Purge the line
steps.why: The line between the coupler and the tap still holds whatever was sitting in it since the last pour, and pushing that straight to a glass is a flat, warm first pint for whoever orders next — purging it here is what makes the first pour off a new keg the same pour as the hundredth.

steps.cue: Leave the door open behind you once the change is logged.
steps.prompt: Leave the door open behind you once the change is logged.
steps.title: Prop the cellar door open on the way out
steps.why: A cellar with the door shut all night has nowhere for any residual CO2 to go; propping it open on the way out is the last control in the chain, and it's the one that protects whoever comes down here next, not you.

steps.cue: Check the lines, the racks and the door before you head back up; click what needs a ticket.

itemNotes.cracked-hose: A hairline crack in a gas hose is a slow leak today and a burst line under a full tank tomorrow — it gets a ticket now, not on the next person's shift.
itemNotes.unlabeled-keg: An empty keg with no 'MT' tag on it looks the same as a full one from across the cellar, which is exactly how someone ends up trying to tap an empty.

steps.prompt: Check the lines, the racks and the door before you head back up; click what needs a ticket.
steps.title: Walk the cellar before you log off
steps.why: The cellar is left the way the next barback needs it to be: nothing cracked, nothing untagged, and the door open behind you — the same discipline the monitor and the chains started the shift with.

tagline: A keg change in the cellar: cylinders chained, the monitor read before entry, coupler off then on, a leak checked at the gauge, the line purged, and the door left open
